title: Bipolar Disorder = "Your Whole Life is Tickets to a Coldplay Concert with Your Boss"
subtitle: A meme for our life and times is also a great metaphor.
body_html:
Oh my. The world of public embarrassment has a new superstar—the (former) CEO of Astronomy, and the Chief People Officer, reacting with embarrassment when captured on the kiss-cam at a Coldplay concert is the “feel-bad” story of the summer. Nothing particularly spectacular was captured—people cheat on their spouses with regularity:

infidelity and divorce rates that approximate 25-50 percent.1

And entitled people do entitled things:

Results are similar for US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) defendants accused of white-collar crimes, and companies with chief executive officers (CEOs) or chief financial officers (CFOs) who use [Ashley Madison] are more than twice as likely to engage in corporate misconduct. The relation is not explained by a wide range of regional, firm, executive, and cultural variables. These findings suggest that personal and workplace behavior are closely related.2

It’s easy, and almost guilt-free, to bask in the schadenfreude when the paragon of “the rules” from HR is caught breaking them.

I have no interest in taking this away from you. It’s been a tough year for many, and we needed a break, in which we could look at people being embarrassed and think: “wow, that is not me.”

However, this moment in time is also a great example of the plight of those suffering from bipolar disorder’s defining mood state, mania, and will take this moment to address it.

For my readers, who, for the sake of the narrative, I will assume are living under a rock, the scene I was referencing above is as follows.

A woman, who is the chief people officer of a company, goes to a Coldplay concert with her boss. They are having an intimate interlude, and are captured on the “kiss cam”—and once they realize they, in their forbidden romance, are on display for the whole concert, they flip out. Which—of course— makes the moment hilarious to the rest of us. It blows up on the internet. The dude loses his CEO job, and his daughter has 10s of millions of views on TikTok. It’s a global-scale embarrassment.

Now, for a moment, imagine you had this sort of thing happen at the scale of your life—and you had a brain disorder that made it impossible to recognize, even in the moment, that being an HR executive and having relations with your boss was a bad idea. Imagine— becoming irritable when someone suggested that maybe you shouldn’t do that and that it might be a bad idea. Imagine you did that whole kiss cam, but NAKED, and screaming all the lyrics to the songs at the same time. We are getting close to the chaos of bipolar mania.

I’m not suggesting either of these individuals had this disorder. However, I’m using this frankly hilarious moment to make a much more somber point: bipolar mania exists. Here is what it looks like:

In bipolar mania, we have a range of symptoms we use a med school mnemonic to recall: DIG FAST.

  • Distractability

  • Indiscretion (like dating one’s boss, or being a boss and deciding it’s time to have a date with your HR lead)

  • Grandiosity

  • Flight Of Ideas

  • Activity (increased, goal-directed)

  • Sleep (decreased need for it)

  • Talkativeness

I propose updating this mnemonic for our life and times, with an updated Bipolar mnemonic: COLDPLAY

  • C – Confident (Grandiosity): Feeling unstoppable or uniquely talented.

  • O – On-the-go (Increased Activity): Excessive goal-directed activity (work, school, socially, sexually).

  • L – Less Sleep Needed: Decreased need for sleep without feeling tired (e.g., 2 hours of sleep and still energetic).

  • D – Distractibility: Easily pulled away by irrelevant stimuli; trouble focusing.

  • P – Pressured Speech: Talking rapidly, loudly, and challenging to interrupt.

  • L – Lack of Inhibition (Impulsivity): Engaging in risky behaviors: spending sprees, sexual indiscretions, reckless driving.

  • A – Accelerated Thoughts (Flight of Ideas): Racing thoughts, ideas jump rapidly from one to another.

  • Y – YOLOing: Making a decision that, although it’s factually true that “You Only Live Once,” has a risk profile that is not in keeping with good judgment.

If you don’t know what bipolar disorder is like, a simple version might be: Imagine you could find yourself in that Coldplay kiss cam moment, without your conscious control. This could happen repeatedly. If you know exactly what bipolar disorder is like, it’s just like the above, except with the sinking feeling of knowing how very realistic that is.

Bipolar mania robs those experiencing it of their insight. You can find yourself in situations where all the evidence is all around you. You could be the chief people officer of your own life—you didn’t just read the handbook, you WROTE IT. And yet, you can find yourself, over and over again, in positions where, despite being endlessly familiar with the rules of decorum and who you’d like to be, you are doing the opposite of what you’d choose for yourself. It’s like looking in a mirror that reflects you, but makes you deny that it’s your reflection. The inability to know your behavior for what it is? That is a core symptom of this state.

Increased sexual behavior is a symptom of mania—politely termed indiscretion. What does that look like?

The sexual outgoing behavior during manic phases was described as joyful, with no feelings of shame connected to it. However, the shifts in sexual drive connected to mood shifts affected the participants’ relationships negatively. Further, all the participants described having outgoing sexual behavior in their youth.

Many bipolar sufferers have a different sense of their sexuality even at baseline:

All participants described having always had a high sex drive compared to friends and sexual partners, also before the first episode of hypomania or mania. In general, their sexuality changed depending on the affective phase they were in. When the participants were hypomanic or manic, they tended to have a higher sex drive, to desire more experimental sex, and they were easily sexually bored. Several participants described their higher sex drive not only as a lust but as a need or kind of internal pressure/urge to have sex.

And in a small study, respondents reported the following, which will be familiar to bipolar sufferers and coldplay fans, alike:

With respect to their sexual lives, four participants described chaotic relations, many partners, and a sexually experimental behavior sometimes exceeding one’s own and others’ boundaries. Alcohol was often involved in sex, and relations were affected by infidelity.3

The more common sexual behavior is also more likely to be risky. There is limited data:

For instance, the number of patients who engaged in recreational drug use and sex at the same time (Q55) was over 40 percent for each group—Bipolar = 46.9 percent (N = 15) versus Comparison = 43.2 percent (N = 19). The percentage of patients who had engaged in sex with a stranger over the last year (Q57) was over 20 percent—Bipolar = 26 percent (N = 8) versus Comparison = 21 percent (N = 8). The number of patients who had engaged in receptive anal and/or vaginal intercourse without condoms with partners not known to be monogamous was 19% (N = 6) for the Bipolar individuals and 8% (N = 3) for the Comparison patients.4

However, the sample sizes are small, so the ability to perform statistical tests on that sample is limited. It is also tough to study because it’s embarrassing.

Bipolar disorder— probably not what was going on with Coldplay, but it wouldn’t have been shocking if it was present. It’s a disabling disorder that frequently presents with sexual behavior that is a bad idea for the individual and others in their life.

It is a mental illness—with a blast radius.

1

Campbell, K., & Wright, D. W. (2010). Marriage today: Exploring the incongruence between Americans’ beliefs and practices. Journal of Comparative Family Studies, 41(3), 329-345.

2

Griffin, J. M., Kruger, S., & Maturana, G. (2019). Personal infidelity and professional conduct in 4 settings. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 116(33), 16268-16273.

3

Krogh HB, Vinberg M, Mortensen GL, Skakke D, Nielsen D, Giraldi A. Bipolar disorder and sexuality: a preliminary qualitative pilot study. Int J Bipolar Disord. 2023 Feb 3;11(1):5. doi: 10.1186/s40345-023-00285-9. PMID: 36735118; PMCID: PMC9898481.

4

Downey J, Friedman RC, Haase E, Goldenberg D, Bell R, Edsall S. Comparison of Sexual Experience and Behavior between Bipolar Outpatients and Outpatients without Mood Disorders. Psychiatry J. 2016;2016:5839181. doi: 10.1155/2016/5839181. Epub 2016 Apr 17. PMID: 27190984; PMCID: PMC4852112.
